source_solutions.independent_solution: Special relativity uses two postulates: every inertial frame has physical laws of the same form, and every inertial frame measures the same vacuum light speed c, independent of the motion of source or receiver relative to that frame. Equality of laws does not require identical measured positions, velocities or trajectories, does not extend this claim to accelerated frames, and does not make the speed of light in all materials equal to c.

The first relativistic postulate extends the classical mechanical relativity principle from mechanical phenomena to all physical processes, including electromagnetic ones, in inertial frames. This is an adopted postulate, not a deduction from mechanics alone; it neither selects a preferred inertial frame nor makes all observed trajectories identical.

Two events are simultaneous in a specified inertial frame exactly when the synchronized clocks local to the two event locations show equal readings at the events, equivalently their coordinate times in that frame agree. Simultaneous receipt of light by one observer is a different condition because travel times may differ. Uncalibrated local clocks and a claim that all frames must agree are not this definition.

For the fixed same pair of events that occur at one location in an inertial frame, a single clock stationary there directly records both events; its elapsed time is the proper time. That proper interval is invariant under a change of description frame. Other relatively moving inertial frames assign this same event pair a longer coordinate-time interval. This does not compare different event pairs or clocks following arbitrary accelerated paths.

Time dilation does not privilege an inertial frame: for a fixed pair of events co-located in K1, K1's one stationary clock records the proper interval, while K assigns a longer coordinate interval. The reciprocal case chooses a different pair of events co-located in K; then K's stationary clock records that pair's proper interval and K1 assigns the longer coordinate interval. Exchanging frame and event roles preserves the same law. Comparing reciprocal cases as if they used one identical event pair is the apparent contradiction; there is no universal absolute slow frame.

The cited experimental test is the decay of short-lived charged pi mesons, not a substituted muon example or Michelson's optical experiment. Their mean proper lifetime is about 2.6e-8 s. For particles moving at constant v before decay, the mean laboratory lifetime is gamma times that mean proper lifetime, where gamma=1/sqrt(1-v^2/c^2), and their mean distance is v times the mean laboratory lifetime when collisions and deceleration are neglected. The result is statistical, not an equal lifetime for every particle. At gamma=10 the speed remains below c; c times the mean proper lifetime gives 7.8 m as a distance scale, not a distance traveled by a resting particle.

source_solutions.independent_solution: For the same rigid rod at rest in an inertial frame its rest/proper length is l0. A frame moving relative to it measures a smaller longitudinal length at nonzero relative speed, equal to l0 at zero relative speed; transverse dimensions are not contracted. Length means endpoint positions recorded simultaneously by the measuring frame's clocks, not apparent visual shape. Rest length is the greatest measured longitudinal length and reciprocal measurements use their respective simultaneity conditions without a preferred inertial frame. The permitted prose refers to equation (8.2) but does not state it, does not provide a quantitative function of v, and does not explicitly establish the monotonic trend across two nonzero speeds. Any demand for that quantitative law or that stronger trend must remain unresolved under this exact whitelist; no formula or extra paragraph is guessed.

For the collinear source law v2=(v1+v)/(1+v1*v/c^2), the classical approximation follows in the stated low-speed regime when both |v| and |v1| are much smaller than c, so |v1*v|/c^2 is negligible and v2 is approximately v1+v. The approximation is not an exact equality for every finite nonzero pair and is not justified merely by both speeds being below c. The source names both low-speed conditions; smallness of only one speed alone is not the stated classical regime.
